scenes.tts: In an earlier lesson you met rhodopsin. It has seven helices holding retinal. Retinal changes shape when it absorbs a photon, and that sets off a G protein. Some microbes have opsins on a similar plan that skip the relay. Channelrhodopsin 2, from a green alga, is itself an ion channel.

scenes.tts: Now shine blue light on channelrhodopsin 2. Blue light changes its retinal. The pore opens within milliseconds. Cations flow into the neuron, with little choice among them. That depolarizes the membrane. At threshold, the neuron fires.

scenes.visual: Large channelrhodopsin-2 block in the membrane. Blue light arrives, the pore opens, cation dots flow in; an idealised voltage sketch rises to a threshold line and the neuron fires.

scenes.tts: Georg Nagel, Peter Hegemann, Ernst Bamberg and colleagues had shown in 2002 and 2003 that channelrhodopsins from the green alga Chlamydomonas are light-gated channels. The same work showed that channelrhodopsin 2 passes cations, and that it works in mammalian cells.

scenes.tts: In 2005 Edward Boyden, Feng Zhang, Ernst Bamberg, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth reported on hippocampal neurons in culture. Given the gene for channelrhodopsin 2, the neurons fired action potentials in step with millisecond flashes of blue light. Other laboratories reported similar results at about the same time.
